summary: David marvels at God's exhaustive knowledge and presence: God knows sitting and rising, words before spoken, formed him in womb, eyes everywhere from heaven to Sheol. He ends with search me, know my heart, lead me in everlasting way — intimacy and accountability.
whyItMatters: Most personal Psalm about being fully known and not running. Answers fear of being unseen or unknowable, and fear of being known and rejected — says both known completely and still sought.

context.author: David
context.literaryForm: Wisdom-tinged personal psalm, with omniscience, omnipresence, omnipotence sections

outline.heading: Where can I flee? Omnipresence — heaven, Sheol, sea
You formed me in womb — fearfully and wonderfully made
Hate for enemies, then search me

keyVerses.text: For the Chief Musician. A Psalm by David. Yahweh, you have searched me, and you know me.
I will give thanks to you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made. Your works are wonderful. My soul knows that very well.
Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts.
keyVerses.why: Turns doctrine into prayer — invitation not just information.

questions.question: Why does David say God knows when I sit and rise and my words before I speak? Comfort or creepy?
questions.answer: Both possible. For David, it's comfort — you're fully known, not overlooked. To be known completely and not abandoned is rare. But he also admits it's too wonderful to grasp (v6). Later he invites search (v23) — so knowledge is not surveillance to punish but intimacy to lead.

questions.question: What does 'Where can I go from your Spirit? If I ascend heaven, make bed in Sheol, you are there'?
questions.answer: Poetic extremes: heaven = high, Sheol = realm of dead (lowest), sea = far edge. No place outside presence. Not that God is everywhere in pantheistic sense, but no escape from attention and availability. For exile or guilt, it's good news and accountability.

questions.question: What about 'fearfully and wonderfully made'? What if someone feels not wonderful due to disability or body image?
questions.answer: Hebrew yare = awe-inspiring, wonderful = distinct, set apart. Not claim everyone feels wonderful, but that making was intentional, watched (v15 in secret, woven). Psalm affirms embodiment — body not mistake. Many with disabilities, trauma find both comfort and struggle here; Psalm doesn't deny struggle, but says you were seen in forming.

questions.question: Why does David suddenly say 'I hate those who hate you' in verses 19-22? Seems jarring.
questions.answer: Imprecatory turn — from intimacy to enemy hate — feels jarring to modern readers. David aligns with God's justice against violent who misuse. He says 'Do I not hate?' inviting God to examine even his hate (v23 search me). Not model for personal revenge but raw honesty bringing even dark emotions into prayer.

questions.question: What does 'search me, know my heart, lead me' at end mean?
questions.answer: After claiming God knows all, David invites what he already said is true — search me. It's willing exposure: test anxious thoughts, see hurtful way, lead to everlasting way. Moves from doctrine (you know) to prayer (keep knowing and leading). Model of vulnerability.

glossary.def: Realm of dead, grave, lowest place — opposite of heaven high.
All-knowing, all-present — theological terms for what Psalm describes poetically.
Hebrew yare — awe-inspiring, reverent wonder, not afraid.
